units.title: Understanding the Command Line
units.tip: The terminal is a text-based interface to your computer. You type commands, the computer executes them and shows results. A shell is the program that reads your commands and talks to the operating system.

exercises.question: What is a shell?
exercises.answer: A program that interprets your text commands and communicates with the operating system
exercises.explain: The shell reads commands you type, translates them into instructions the OS understands, and displays the results. Bash and Zsh are popular shells.
choices: A program that interprets your text commands and communicates with the operating system

exercises.question: What does the dollar sign ($) at the start of a terminal line represent?
exercises.answer: The command prompt, where you type commands
exercises.explain: The shell displays $ (or # for root) to show it is ready for input. Everything after $ is the command you type.
choices: The command prompt, where you type commands

exercises.question: What is the current working directory in a terminal?
exercises.answer: The folder where commands execute and files are accessed by default
exercises.explain: Your shell always operates from a specific folder. Commands work relative to this location unless you specify a full path.
choices: The folder where commands execute and files are accessed by default

exercises.question: What does pwd stand for?
exercises.answer: Print Working Directory
exercises.explain: pwd displays the full path to the current folder. Use it to confirm where you are in the file system.

exercises.question: What does cd do?
exercises.answer: Changes the current working directory to another folder
exercises.explain: cd stands for Change Directory. Type cd followed by a folder name or path to move into that folder.
choices: Changes the current working directory to another folder

exercises.question: What does ls do?
exercises.answer: Lists the files and folders in the current directory
exercises.explain: ls shows all visible items in the current folder. Add flags like -a to show hidden files or -l for detailed information.
choices: Lists the files and folders in the current directory

exercises.question: What is an absolute path?
exercises.answer: A path that starts from the root (/) and specifies the complete location
exercises.explain: An absolute path shows the full route from the root directory. Example: /Users/joshua/Documents/file.txt works from anywhere.
choices: A path starting from the home folder
A path that starts from the root (/) and specifies the complete location
A path that uses special characters

exercises.question: What is a relative path?
exercises.answer: A path specified from the current working directory
exercises.explain: Relative paths work from where you are now. Example: if you are in Documents, typing ./file.txt refers to file.txt in the current folder.
choices: A path specified from the current working directory
A path used only in Git

exercises.question: What does the tilde (~) represent in a terminal path?
exercises.answer: Your home directory
exercises.explain: ~ is a shortcut for your user's home folder. Typing cd ~ takes you home from anywhere.

exercises.question: What do the two dots (..) mean in a path?
exercises.answer: Go up one level to the parent directory
exercises.explain: .. is a shortcut to the folder above the current one. cd .. moves up one level in the folder hierarchy.
choices: Go up one level to the parent directory
Go to the last folder you visited

units.title: Working with Files and Directories
units.tip: You can create, copy, move, and delete files entirely from the terminal. Understanding these commands and redirection lets you work with data efficiently without a graphical interface.

exercises.question: What does mkdir do?
exercises.answer: Creates a new directory (folder)
exercises.explain: mkdir stands for Make Directory. Use mkdir foldername to create a new folder in the current location.

exercises.question: What does cp do?
exercises.answer: Copies a file or directory
exercises.explain: cp copies files or folders. Use cp source destination to create a copy. Add -r flag to copy entire directories.

exercises.question: What does mv do?
exercises.answer: Moves or renames a file or directory
exercises.explain: mv moves files between folders or renames them. Use mv oldname newname to rename, or mv file folder/ to move.
choices: Moves or renames a file or directory

exercises.question: What does rm do?
exercises.answer: Removes (deletes) a file
exercises.explain: rm deletes files permanently. Be careful: deleted files cannot be recovered. Add -r to delete directories with contents.

exercises.question: What does cat do?
exercises.answer: Displays the contents of a file in the terminal
exercises.explain: cat shows file contents on screen. Use cat filename to view a text file. It is short for concatenate.
choices: Displays the contents of a file in the terminal

exercises.question: What does the pipe (|) operator do?
exercises.answer: Sends the output of one command as input to another command
exercises.explain: Pipes chain commands together. Example: cat file.txt | grep word finds lines containing a word in a file.
choices: Sends the output of one command as input to another command

exercises.question: What does the > operator do?
exercises.answer: Redirects output to a file, overwriting it
exercises.explain: The > symbol saves command output to a file. Example: echo hello > file.txt creates file.txt with hello inside.
choices: Redirects output to a file, overwriting it
Checks if output is larger than input

exercises.question: What does the >> operator do?
exercises.answer: Appends output to the end of a file
exercises.explain: >> adds new content to the end of a file without deleting what is there. Example: echo world >> file.txt adds world to the end.
choices: Appends output to the end of a file

exercises.question: What does the < operator do?
exercises.answer: Sends the contents of a file as input to a command
exercises.explain: The < symbol redirects a file as input. Example: grep word < file.txt searches for word inside file.txt.
choices: Checks if input is smaller than output
Sends the contents of a file as input to a command

exercises.question: In the command grep pattern file.txt | sort, what happens?
exercises.answer: grep finds lines, then sort arranges them alphabetically
exercises.explain: grep finds all matching lines in file.txt, then the pipe (|) sends those lines to sort, which orders them.
choices: grep finds lines, then sort arranges them alphabetically
Both commands run at the same time
Only grep executes; sort is ignored

units.title: Introducing Git Concepts
units.tip: Git is a version control system that tracks changes to files. A repository stores your entire project history. Your working tree is where you edit files. The staging area is where you prepare changes before saving them.

exercises.question: What is a Git repository?
exercises.answer: A directory that contains your project and its entire version history
exercises.explain: A repository (repo) stores all your files, changes, and history. It includes a hidden .git folder with all version information.
choices: A directory that contains your project and its entire version history

exercises.question: What is a commit?
exercises.answer: A snapshot of changes saved with a descriptive message
exercises.explain: A commit records what changed, who made the change, and when. It is like saving a labeled version of your project.
choices: A snapshot of changes saved with a descriptive message
A backup of the entire repository

exercises.question: What is the working tree in Git?
exercises.answer: The actual files and folders in your directory that you edit
exercises.explain: The working tree is where you see and modify files. It is different from the Git history stored in .git.
choices: The actual files and folders in your directory that you edit

exercises.question: What is the staging area?
exercises.answer: A temporary holding area where you select which changes to commit
exercises.explain: The staging area (also called the index) lets you choose which edits to include in the next commit.
choices: A temporary holding area where you select which changes to commit

exercises.question: What does the .git folder contain?
exercises.answer: All version history, metadata, and configuration for the repository
exercises.explain: The .git folder (hidden by default) stores commits, branches, configuration, and everything Git needs to track your project.
choices: All version history, metadata, and configuration for the repository

exercises.question: In Git, what is the typical sequence: edit files, ?, commit?
exercises.answer: Stage changes with git add
exercises.explain: The workflow is: edit files, stage them with git add, then commit. This lets you choose what goes in each commit.

exercises.question: What does git status show?
exercises.answer: Which files have changed and which are staged for commit
exercises.explain: git status tells you the current state: modified files, untracked files, and what is in the staging area.
choices: Which files have changed and which are staged for commit

exercises.question: What does git add filename do?
exercises.answer: Stages the file for the next commit
exercises.explain: git add places a modified or new file into the staging area. You can then commit all staged changes together.
choices: Stages the file for the next commit
Uploads the file to the server

exercises.question: What does git commit -m "message" do?
exercises.answer: Saves all staged changes as a commit with a description
exercises.explain: git commit creates a snapshot. The -m flag lets you add a message describing the changes.
choices: Saves all staged changes as a commit with a description

exercises.question: What does git log show?
exercises.answer: A history of all commits with messages and timestamps
exercises.explain: git log displays the commit history in reverse order (newest first). Each entry shows the author, date, and message.
choices: A history of all commits with messages and timestamps

units.title: Daily Git Commands
units.tip: Once you understand the basics, everyday Git work involves initializing repositories, cloning existing ones, viewing differences, and managing changes. These commands are the foundation of collaborative development.

exercises.question: What does git init do?
exercises.answer: Creates a new empty Git repository in the current directory
exercises.explain: git init sets up a .git folder and prepares the directory for version control.
choices: Initializes a connection to a server
Creates a new empty Git repository in the current directory

exercises.question: What does git clone url do?
exercises.answer: Downloads an entire repository from a server and copies it locally
exercises.explain: git clone gets a full copy of a project, including all history and branches, from a remote location.
choices: Downloads an entire repository from a server and copies it locally

exercises.question: What does git diff show?
exercises.answer: Changes in your working tree that you have not staged yet
exercises.explain: Plain git diff compares your files to the staging area, so it shows edits you have not staged. Use git diff --staged to see what is staged for the next commit.
choices: Changes in your working tree that you have not staged yet

exercises.question: What does git show commitid do?
exercises.answer: Displays the changes made in a specific commit
exercises.explain: git show lets you see what changed in a particular commit, including the message and diff.
choices: Displays the changes made in a specific commit

exercises.question: What does git add . do?
exercises.answer: Stages all modified and new files for the next commit
exercises.explain: git add . (dot) stages every change in the current directory and subdirectories.
choices: Stages all modified and new files for the next commit

exercises.question: What does git restore filename do?
exercises.answer: Discards changes to a file and restores the last committed version
exercises.explain: git restore reverts a file to its state in the last commit. Unsaved changes are lost.
choices: Discards changes to a file and restores the last committed version

exercises.question: What does git reset HEAD filename do?
exercises.answer: Unstages a file that was added to the staging area
exercises.explain: git reset removes a file from the staging area without changing your working tree.
choices: Unstages a file that was added to the staging area

exercises.question: What does the command git log --oneline do?
exercises.answer: Shows the commit history with one commit per line and short hashes
exercises.explain: The --oneline flag makes git log compact and readable, showing just the commit hash and message.
choices: Shows the commit history with one commit per line and short hashes

exercises.question: What should you do before committing?
exercises.answer: Review your changes with git diff and git status
exercises.explain: Always check what you are committing to catch mistakes and write accurate messages.
choices: Review your changes with git diff and git status

exercises.question: What makes a good commit message?
exercises.answer: Short, clear, and describes what changed and why
exercises.explain: Good messages start with a verb (Add, Fix, Refactor) and explain the purpose. Avoid vague messages like update or changes.
choices: Short, clear, and describes what changed and why

units.title: Branches and Merging
units.tip: Branches let you work on separate features without affecting the main code. You can create, switch between, and merge branches. Merge conflicts happen when two branches change the same lines, and you must resolve them manually.

exercises.question: What is a branch in Git?
exercises.answer: A separate line of development that diverges from the main code
exercises.explain: Branches let multiple developers work on different features simultaneously without interfering.
choices: A backup of the entire project
A separate line of development that diverges from the main code

exercises.question: What does git branch do?
exercises.answer: Lists all local branches or creates a new branch
exercises.explain: git branch with no arguments lists branches. git branch name creates a new branch.
choices: Lists all local branches or creates a new branch

exercises.question: What does git switch branchname do?
exercises.answer: Changes your working tree to a different branch
exercises.explain: git switch moves you to another branch. Your files update to match that branch's state.
choices: Changes your working tree to a different branch

exercises.question: What does git branch -d branchname do?
exercises.answer: Deletes a local branch
exercises.explain: git branch -d removes a branch. Use -D (capital) to force delete even if not merged.

exercises.question: What does git switch -c branchname do?
exercises.answer: Creates a new branch and switches to it immediately
exercises.explain: git switch -c (create) does both steps at once. You start working on the new branch right away.
choices: Creates a new branch and switches to it immediately

exercises.question: What does git merge branchname do?
exercises.answer: Combines the changes from another branch into the current branch
exercises.explain: git merge integrates commits from one branch into your current branch. Usually you merge features back into main.
choices: Combines the changes from another branch into the current branch

exercises.question: What is a merge conflict?
exercises.answer: A situation where two branches changed the same lines and Git cannot automatically merge
exercises.explain: Conflicts happen when different commits modify overlapping code. You must manually choose which changes to keep.
choices: A situation where two branches changed the same lines and Git cannot automatically merge

exercises.question: What do the conflict markers <<<<<<, ======, and >>>>>> indicate?
exercises.answer: The boundaries between conflicting versions that need to be resolved
exercises.explain: These markers show your version (between <<<< and ====) and the other branch's version (between ==== and >>>>).
choices: The boundaries between conflicting versions that need to be resolved

exercises.question: How do you resolve a merge conflict?
exercises.answer: Edit the conflicted files, remove conflict markers, choose which changes to keep, then add and commit
exercises.explain: Open the conflicted files, manually choose between versions or combine them, delete the markers, stage, and commit.
choices: Edit the conflicted files, remove conflict markers, choose which changes to keep, then add and commit

exercises.question: What is a fast-forward merge?
exercises.answer: A merge where the target branch has no new commits, so history is linear
exercises.explain: A fast-forward merge happens when one branch is directly ahead of another with no diverging commits.
choices: A merge that is faster than normal
A merge where the target branch has no new commits, so history is linear
A merge that requires conflict resolution

units.title: Remotes and Teamwork
units.tip: A remote is a version of your repository on a server like GitHub. Push sends your commits to the remote. Pull gets commits from others. Fetch downloads without merging. Pull requests are proposals to merge branches and integrate team changes.

exercises.question: What is a remote in Git?
exercises.answer: A version of your repository on a server, usually a central shared location
exercises.explain: Remotes let teams share code. origin is the default remote, usually pointing to GitHub or another server.
choices: A backup copy on your computer
A version of your repository on a server, usually a central shared location

exercises.question: What does git remote -v do?
exercises.answer: Shows the addresses of all configured remotes
exercises.explain: git remote -v (verbose) displays remote names and URLs. Most projects have origin pointing to their main server.
choices: Shows the addresses of all configured remotes

exercises.question: What does git push origin branchname do?
exercises.answer: Uploads your commits to the remote server on the specified branch
exercises.explain: git push sends your local commits to the remote. origin is the remote, branchname is the target branch.
choices: Uploads your commits to the remote server on the specified branch

exercises.question: What does git pull do?
exercises.answer: Fetches commits from the remote and merges them into your current branch
exercises.explain: git pull is equivalent to git fetch followed by git merge. It updates your branch with remote changes.
choices: Fetches commits from the remote and merges them into your current branch

exercises.question: What does git fetch do?
exercises.answer: Downloads commits from the remote without merging
exercises.explain: git fetch gets new commits from the server and updates remote tracking branches. Use it to see what others have done before merging.
choices: Downloads commits from the remote without merging

exercises.question: What is a pull request?
exercises.answer: A proposal to merge one branch into another, usually for code review before merging
exercises.explain: Pull requests let teams review changes, discuss improvements, and approve before integrating into main.
choices: A proposal to merge one branch into another, usually for code review before merging

exercises.question: On which platform do you create a pull request?
exercises.answer: The web interface of the hosting service (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket)
exercises.explain: Pull requests are created on the server interface, not from the terminal. They live alongside your code online.
choices: In the terminal with git pr
The web interface of the hosting service (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket)

exercises.question: What should you do before creating a pull request?
exercises.answer: Push your branch, ensure commits are clean, and verify changes work
exercises.explain: Review your commits, test your changes, and push to the remote before opening a pull request.
choices: Push your branch, ensure commits are clean, and verify changes work

exercises.question: What does a code review in a pull request involve?
exercises.answer: Team members checking the changes, discussing improvements, and approving before merge
exercises.explain: Code reviews catch bugs, ensure quality, share knowledge, and maintain standards.
choices: Team members checking the changes, discussing improvements, and approving before merge

exercises.question: What is the typical workflow: create feature branch, make changes, ?, merge?
exercises.answer: Push to remote and create a pull request for review
exercises.explain: After commits, push your branch and create a pull request. Team members review, then merge to main.
choices: Push to remote and create a pull request for review
